name: rathole
popularity: 14.2k stars, 827 forks, 73 watchers; widely used as an frp/ngrok alternative, Docker Hub image (rapiz1/rathole) with active pulls, active Gitter chat community
maturity: Actively maintained (234 commits, ongoing releases with semver tags and CI badge); no obvious red flags, but the project's own 'Planning' section lists 'HTTP APIs for configuration' as still work-in-progress (not yet shipped), so dynamic/API-driven tunnel registration is not fully available today (hot-reload via config file is supported instead).
client_requirements: Single static Rust binary (~500KiB minimal build) for both client and server, no TAP/TUN interface, no admin/root required, no complex install — just run the binary with a TOML config. Meets constraints well.
server_requirements: Full server source code available (same repo, Rust). Server is config-file (TOML) driven with hot-reload of the config file; a built-in HTTP control-plane API is explicitly listed as 'WIP' / planned but not confirmed shipped, so today it is essentially a config-driven binary, not a REST API you can hit to register tunnels programmatically.
has_programmable_api: false — an HTTP API for configuration is only planned/WIP per the README, not a confirmed shipped feature; current control is via TOML config file hot-reload only.
viability_notes: Excellent fit on the client side (tiny static binary, no admin, no TUN) and server source is open and lightweight, but lacks a confirmed working HTTP control-plane API today, meaning our SvelteKit backend would have to manage tunnels by writing/hot-reloading TOML config files rather than calling a REST API. Good fallback option if we're willing to shell out to config-file management.

name: sshuttle
popularity: 13.6k stars, 794 forks, 134 watchers; long-standing popular 'poor man's VPN' tool, widely referenced in sysadmin/security tooling lists
maturity: Actively maintained (1,363 commits, ongoing releases, uses modern tooling like uv/pyproject.toml); mature and stable project with no major red flags for its intended use case.
client_requirements: FAILS constraint. Despite README claims of 'doesn't require admin', sshuttle works as a transparent proxy/VPN-like tool: it uses iptables/pf firewall rules and typically must run the local sshuttle process as root (or with sudo) on the client to set up NAT/firewall redirection to route all matching traffic through the SSH tunnel; on the client it needs elevated privileges to manipulate the routing/firewall tables, which is effectively equivalent to VPN-style setup even though it avoids a literal TUN/TAP kernel driver in most modes. This is a fundamentally different (transparent-proxy) usage model than a simple reverse tunnel client, and not what we need.
server_requirements: Server-side just needs plain SSH access (uses the remote user's Python via SSH, no separate daemon/API); no server source needed beyond stock sshd — but this is irrelevant given the client fails our hard constraint.
server_language: Python (assembled/pushed over SSH at connect time)
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP API; it's purely a CLI wrapping SSH + local firewall manipulation.
viability_notes: sshuttle is architecturally a whole-network transparent VPN-like proxy, not a single-service reverse tunnel; its client requires root/admin to configure firewall/NAT rules, directly violating our no-admin constraint. Also has no programmable server API — it's just SSH. Not suitable for our use case.

name: bore
popularity: 11.5k stars, 528 forks, 62 watchers; packaged on Homebrew, AUR, Gentoo overlay, crates.io (bore-cli), public hosted instance at bore.pub
maturity: Actively maintained relative to its scope (68 commits — intentionally minimal, ~400 lines of code); has CI, versioned Docker images and crates.io releases. No red flags, but it is a deliberately minimal project (no plans for a control-plane API, by design philosophy of doing 'one thing').
client_requirements: Single static Rust binary (`bore local <port> --to <server>`), installable via Homebrew/AUR/Cargo/prebuilt release binaries or Docker. No TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed. Excellent fit.
server_requirements: Full server source available (same repo). Server is a single binary (`bore server`) configured entirely via CLI flags/env vars (min/max port range, bind address, optional shared secret) — no config file and no HTTP control-plane/REST API at all; tunnels are created dynamically by the client itself via the control-port protocol (not by pushing registrations from an external system).
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP/REST API; only a lightweight custom TCP control protocol between client and server, driven from the client side, not something a SvelteKit backend can call directly to register tunnels for other machines.
viability_notes: Ideal on the client side (trivial static binary, no admin, no TUN) and the server is fully open-source and simple to self-host, but there is no HTTP control-plane/API to register or manage tunnels from our own backend — tunnel creation is driven only by the client's own connection to the server. Good if our backend can just tell the client to run 'bore local', less good if we need central orchestration.

name: gost
popularity: 7.5k stars, 828 forks, 52 watchers; large multi-protocol proxy/tunnel toolkit with companion GUI (gostctl) and WebUI (gost-ui) projects, active Telegram/Google Group community
maturity: Actively maintained (558 commits, continuous releases, install script, Docker images, dedicated docs site gost.run); broad protocol support (websocket, grpc, quic, kcp, etc.) and a documented Web API — no major red flags.
client_requirements: Single Go binary, installable via releases page, install script, or Docker; used as a reverse-proxy/tunnel client with no admin/root required. Note: gost ALSO supports optional TUN/TAP device modes for VPN-like use cases, but that is an optional feature — for a plain reverse-proxy/tunnel client (websocket/TCP forwarding) it runs as a normal unprivileged process. Meets constraints as long as TUN/TAP mode is avoided.
server_requirements: Full server source available (same repo, Go). Server exposes a genuine RESTful Web API (`-api` flag or `api:` config block) with HTTP Basic Auth, configurable path prefix, access logging, and a built-in Swagger/OpenAPI spec (testable at api.gost.run/swagger-ui) for dynamically creating/listing/removing services, listeners, and chains at runtime — this is a real hittable control-plane, not just a config file.
has_programmable_api: true — Go server with a documented RESTful HTTP API (Basic Auth, Swagger/OpenAPI spec) for dynamic runtime configuration of services/tunnels; can be called from any backend including a SvelteKit/Node app via plain HTTP requests.
viability_notes: Strong candidate: single unprivileged Go binary client, open server source, and a real documented REST API with Swagger docs for dynamically registering tunnels/services — exactly the kind of control-plane we want to hit from SvelteKit. Slight complexity cost is gost's very large feature surface (many protocols/concepts to learn) versus more minimal tools.

name: tunnelto
popularity: 7.1k stars, 546 forks, 49 watchers; published on crates.io as 'wormhole-tunnel'/'tunnelto', Homebrew tap, Docker image, hosted commercial service at tunnelto.dev
maturity: Moderate activity (119 commits); README shows Cargo.toml pinned near v0.1.14 and a note that self-hosted deployments do not support multi-instance/centralized coordination (the real distributed version is proprietary, running on fly.io). This is a meaningful limitation/red flag for production self-hosting at scale, though basic single-instance self-hosting works.
client_requirements: Single Rust binary installable via Homebrew, Cargo, or prebuilt release download. No TAP/TUN, no admin/root. Good fit.
server_requirements: Server source available (tunnelto_server crate in the same repo), configured via environment variables, with a documented but caveated self-host path (must build for musl target via provided script, run behind Docker/alpine). No HTTP REST control-plane API is documented for registering tunnels externally — tunnels are established by the client's own websocket connection to the control port; self-hosted deployments explicitly don't support multiple server instances/centralized coordination (that's proprietary in the hosted fly.io version).
has_programmable_api: false — no documented external REST API; tunnel registration happens via the client's own control-websocket handshake with the server, and multi-instance orchestration is a proprietary feature of the hosted service, not available in the OSS self-hosted server.
viability_notes: Client is simple and admin-free, but the self-hosted server explicitly lacks the distributed/coordination capability of the commercial hosted version and has no programmable control-plane API — plus lower commit activity than peers. Usable for a single-instance self-hosted deployment but a weaker choice than gost/rathole/bore for programmatic orchestration.

name: zrok
popularity: 4.7k stars, 222 forks, 30 watchers; backed by the OpenZiti project/NetFoundry, has a hosted zrok.io service, active YouTube 'office hours' series, large commit history (4,281 commits)
maturity: Very actively maintained (huge commit volume, frequent releases, dedicated docs site docs.zrok.io, self-hosting guide, and a website/UI subproject); no red flags — one of the more professionally maintained projects in this batch.
client_requirements: Single binary (zrok CLI) across Windows/macOS/Linux/Raspberry Pi; built on OpenZiti's zero-trust overlay but does NOT require a traditional TUN/TAP virtual NIC or admin/root for basic HTTP/TCP share/access commands — it operates as a userspace SDK-driven client. Meets constraints for typical share/access use, though OpenZiti's broader ecosystem does have optional TUN-based 'ziti-edge-tunnel' clients for full VPN-style use that would NOT meet the constraint if chosen instead.
server_requirements: Full server (controller + edge components) source available in the same repo (Go); single binary can contain the whole self-hosted service per the README ('Single binary contains everything you need'). Also ships a Go SDK (`sdk.CreateShare`, `sdk.NewListener`) for embedding zrok sharing directly into applications, and a REST API (rest_client_zrok/rest_server_zrok/rest_model_zrok directories generated from an OpenAPI spec) that a backend could call to create/manage shares programmatically.
has_programmable_api: true — Go SDK for embedding sharing/tunnel logic, plus a generated REST client/server (OpenAPI-based) for the zrok controller that exposes share creation/management over HTTP; callable from a SvelteKit backend via plain HTTP even though no first-party JS/TS client is provided (would need to hit the REST endpoints directly or generate a TS client from the OpenAPI spec).
viability_notes: Strong option: admin-free single-binary client, fully open server source, actively maintained by a serious team, and a genuine REST API + Go SDK for programmatic share management. Slightly more architecturally complex than rathole/bore (built atop the OpenZiti zero-trust overlay, controller+edge-router topology) which adds self-hosting overhead, but well worth serious evaluation for its control-plane API.

name: expose
popularity: 4.6k stars, 308 forks, 57 watchers; published on Packagist (beyondcode/expose), has a commercial hosted 'Expose Pro' offering
maturity: Repo has moved/renamed to exposedev/expose (beyondcode/expose redirects there); 730 commits total but the README pushes users primarily toward the managed/paid Expose Pro service rather than self-hosting, which is a mild red flag for how well-supported pure self-hosting is going forward.
client_requirements: PHP-based CLI (installed via Composer / PHAR, or the 'expose' bash wrapper script); no TAP/TUN or admin/root needed to run the client, but it does require a PHP runtime to be present, which is a heavier dependency than a single static binary (though still not 'complex install' in the VPN-driver sense).
server_requirements: Server source is available (same Laravel-based PHP app, same repo) and can self-host via Docker/Docker Compose, but it is a full Laravel application (database, queue workers, internal dashboard) rather than a lightweight single binary — heavier operational footprint than the Go/Rust tools in this batch. No public documentation of a simple external REST API for tunnel registration was found beyond its own internal Laravel-based dashboard/DB models.
has_programmable_api: false (not confirmed) — no documented standalone HTTP API separate from the full Laravel app's internal database/dashboard; self-hosting requires running an entire Laravel stack rather than a lightweight service you'd script against externally.
viability_notes: Client-side is workable (no admin/TUN) but requires a PHP runtime rather than a static binary, and the self-hosted server is a full Laravel application (DB, queues) with the project steering users toward its paid managed 'Expose Pro' service — heavier and less API-friendly than the Go/Rust alternatives in this batch.

name: pgrok
popularity: 3.6k stars, 131 forks, 20 watchers; smaller but growing project, listed on Sourcegraph, has sponsor (Bytebase)
maturity: Actively developed (276 commits, recent tooling like .claude/.agents skill directories suggesting current work), positions itself explicitly as a 'poor man's ngrok' for small teams; author is upfront that it's not meant for production SLAs, which is a reasonable but notable caveat/red flag for anything beyond internal/dev use.
client_requirements: Single Go binary (`pgrok`), installable via Homebrew or prebuilt release archive; can even be replaced entirely by a vanilla `ssh -R` command since it's just SSH remote port forwarding under the hood. No TAP/TUN, no admin/root required. Excellent fit.
server_requirements: Full server source available (`pgrokd`, same repo, Go); requires a PostgreSQL database and an OIDC/SSO provider for auth, plus a reverse proxy (Caddy) in front — more moving parts to self-host than rathole/bore/gost. It is fundamentally an SSH remote-port-forwarding relay with OIDC-gated web login to obtain tokens/URLs; no standalone REST/HTTP control-plane API for external tunnel registration is documented — tunnels are created by users authenticating via the web UI/SSO then running the client, not by an external system calling an API.
has_programmable_api: false — no documented REST API for programmatic tunnel registration; provisioning flow is web-UI/OIDC-login driven, then SSH remote-port-forward for the actual tunnel.
viability_notes: Client side is great (single Go binary, or even vanilla SSH, no admin needed), but the server requires Postgres + an OIDC/SSO provider + reverse proxy, and has no programmable API — its whole design assumes human users authenticating via SSO rather than a backend registering tunnels for them. Heavier and less scriptable than gost or zrok for our use case.
